newsitem.title: UK: UK to reveal sex offender names in high-risk cases.
newsitem.headline: UK to reveal sex offender names in high-risk cases.

text.p: Britain announced new guidelines on Monday to allow police to warn people when a convicted paedophile moves into their area.
Sex offenders will be required to inform authorities where they live and if they change their name or address.
The police will be able to pass on details to employers, community organisations and the public if the abuser is considered a genuine threat to children.
But the new policy stopped short of the full disclosure demanded by some pressure groups.
The government's move came in response to a growing tide of vigilante behaviour in communities upset at what some see as lenient prison terms for sex offenders.
Anti-paedophile demonstrations have broken out across Britain in the last year and in some instances known offenders have been driven from their homes.
The government expressed concern that a blanket policy of exposing paedophiles' identities would push sex offenders underground.
"They could disappear from view, no longer receive treatment they need and pose a threat to yet more children," Home Office (Interior Ministry) Minister Alun Michael said in a statement.
In one case, a convicted couple were forced to move three times in seven months after police revealed their identities to residents.

The couple sued but Britain's High Court ruled the police had acted legally in revealing their name and address, although it said a general policy of identifying abusers could never be justified. The case paved the way for the government ruling.
The guidelines coincide with the launch next month of a national sex offenders' register that will enable police to track paedophiles and other sex offenders around the country.
Failing to register could bring a jail term of up to six months and a 5,000 pound ($7,930) fine.
As offenders are convicted, their last known address will be entered on a police computer database. Once they leave prison, any change of address will be logged.
Under the act, anyone jailed for a sex offence will be entered on the register for a period ranging from five years to life depending on the severity of the crime.

Similar measures, dubbed "Megan's Laws" after a seven-year-old girl who was raped and murdered, have been adopted in the United States, with some states going a step further by requiring public notification of sex offenders' identities.
The policy has been linked to death threats, firebombings and beatings. Some cases involved mistaken identities.
The state of California recently launched a CD-ROM of more than 63,000 registered sex offenders for public use. ($ = 0.630 British Pounds)
